opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've come to feel pretty strongly about over the years. When you're designing an attack, there's a huge temptation to get clever with the loss function. You think, "I understand this defense, so I'll write a loss that captures exactly what I want." In my experience that almost always makes things worse.

The reason is that the hard part of an attack is usually not specifying the objective. It's the optimization. Gradient descent is a remarkably powerful tool, but only when the landscape is reasonably well-behaved. Every term you add, every weighting constant, every clever trick to handle some edge case, makes the landscape harder to optimize. You end up with a bunch of hyperparameters that interact in strange ways, and when the attack fails you can't tell whether the model is actually robust or you just got the balance wrong.

With a simple loss, like "make the logit of the target class bigger than everything else by some margin," you know what you're optimizing. If it doesn't work, you can debug it. You can look at the loss curve and see whether it's stuck, whether gradients are vanishing, whether something is being masked. That diagnostic clarity is worth an enormous amount.

There's also a robustness argument. Many defenses that looked strong were evaluated with attacks that were too complicated or poorly tuned. When someone came along with a straightforward, well-optimized attack, they fell apart. So I try to start with the simplest thing that could work, run it for a lot of iterations, and only add complexity when I have concrete evidence that I need it, like a gradient-masking issue I have to route around.

And honestly, there's a meta-lesson here that goes beyond adversarial examples. A lot of machine learning progress comes from people trying the dumb, simple thing and scaling it, rather than engineering something elaborate. I'd rather spend my effort making the optimization work well than making the objective look sophisticated.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a simple loss makes failures easier to debug and lets you inspect the loss curve and gradients.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say that the last few percentage points of attack success are often unnecessary.

fable-5.1.text:
Mostly because the loss function is the one thing you're actually optimizing, and if you make it complicated you lose the ability to reason about what the optimizer is doing. When an attack fails, I want to know whether it failed because the model is genuinely robust or because I built a bad objective. With something like a plain margin loss on the logits, or even just cross-entropy, I can look at the loss curve and tell you exactly what's happening. If it's flat, the gradients are probably masked or the model is non-differentiable somewhere. If it's going down but the attack still isn't succeeding, I've probably got a bug in the constraint handling. Every term you add is another place for a mistake to hide.

The other thing is that the fancy losses almost never buy you anything. People will stack three or four regularizers and a perceptual term and a confidence weighting, and then when you ablate it, the simple version does just as well or better. A lot of the perceived advantage comes from the fact that they tuned the complicated one and didn't bother tuning the simple one. If you give cross-entropy the same number of steps and a reasonable step size, it tends to be very competitive.

And there's a subtle failure mode where a complex loss can be optimizing something other than what you care about. You think you're maximizing misclassification, but really you're minimizing some surrogate that saturates early, and the optimizer happily sits in a region where the surrogate looks great and the model is still correct. Cross-entropy has exactly that problem too, actually, which is why I tend to prefer the logit margin, but the point is you want a loss where you can state in one sentence what it's measuring and check that it's actually measuring it.

So the heuristic is: start with the dumbest thing that could possibly work, make it work, and only add complexity when you have a concrete reason that the simple thing is failing. In my experience that reason shows up a lot less often than people expect.

r001.rationale: The response says simple losses make it easier to reason about optimizer behavior and diagnose whether a failed attack reflects model robustness, a bad objective, or a bug.

r002.rationale: It says simple losses often perform as well as or better than complicated ones, but does not state that pursuing the last few percentage points of attack success is often unnecessary.

astra-6.text:
I tend to favor simple loss functions because, when an attack doesn’t work, I want to understand why. If you’ve built a complicated objective with lots of terms and hyperparameters, it’s hard to tell whether the model is actually robust or whether your optimization is just failing.

For example, if I want the model to classify an image as a particular target class, a very direct objective is to make that class’s score larger than the scores of all the other classes. That closely matches what I’m trying to accomplish, and it gives me something straightforward to debug.

That doesn’t mean a simple loss is always best. But I like to start there and add complexity when there’s a specific failure that the complexity fixes. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of effort tuning the attack without learning much about the model.

r001.rationale: The response says simple objectives make attack failures easier to understand and provide something straightforward to debug.

r002.rationale: It does not state that achieving the last few percentage points of attack success is often unnecessary.

sol-6.1.text:
The main reason is that when an attack fails, I want to understand why. If I’ve built a complicated loss function with a bunch of terms and tricks, it’s hard to tell whether the defense is actually robust or whether I’ve just made the optimization problem difficult.

So I usually start with the simplest objective that captures what I want: make the wrong answer score higher than the right answer. Then I can look at whether gradient descent is making progress and diagnose what’s going on. If there’s a specific reason that objective doesn’t work, I’ll add complexity to address it. But I want each piece to have a reason to exist. Otherwise, you risk mistaking a weakness in your attack for evidence that the model is secure.
